@WhiskeyWonderer > the government has the final say on how high interest rates go
Technically true, but in practice almost completely irrelevant.  They _can_ set interest rates to whatever they want of course, but they're generally constrained by the (expected) outcome of any change.  Set it too low and inflation skyrockets.  Set it too high and the economy stalls out.

That's where the fragility comes in.  Anything that forces the government to change interest rates more than percent or so (like say, a singularly insane president that imposes tariffs on basically everything from everywhere and then turns around and breaks a significant fraction of the world's energy supply) starts causing serious problems and risks of recession.

2-3% is considered the "sweet spot" (though the exact number is fairly empirical - that it is comes from trial-and-error rather than being derived from first principles).  5% is a massive stretch, and when it goes much higher than that, the economy essentially stops growing and bad things happen.

To be fair, a lot of the "problem" is simply that we insist on infinite growth.  We're unwilling to accept tomorrow being just as good as today - it always has to be _better_ than today or we start clamoring about the end of the world.  That is, when put so bluntly, an obviously stupid ideology but unfortunately its the one the world runs on and until that changes, economies everywhere will continue to be pretty fragile. Its considered a "worst possible outcome" because the central banks have no way to get out of it without breaking something else.  Their primary tool is setting the interest rate, but they end up in a situation where:
- If they raise the interest rate, they help slow inflation but they also further slow productivity.
- If they lower the interest rate, they help increase productivity but also trigger more inflation.

A similar argument applies to printing more money and pretty much every other tool they have available.  Stagflation ties productivity to the inflation rate (indirectly, but nonetheless effectively) in almost all aspects.  Making one better makes the other worse, and both sides lead to even worse short-term outcomes.

Its not good.  Japan's being force out of stagflation and into full-on recession first by covid and then by Trump's insane trade policies causing skyrocketing inflation (and forcing governments - including Japan - to raise interest rates to compensate).  Long-term this will _probably_ be better for Japan as a crash also acts as a reset, but their debt load is extremely challenging to put it politely, and "long-term" could be very long indeed.

At the same time, Trump's rapidly driving the US into a stagflation state (arguably already there). That's where your arguments around "private sector sentiment" start to fall apart.  For-profit businesses operate specifically _for profit._  There is not any great difference between a Japanese business and an American business when it comes to risk management. text:
@WhiskeyWonderer > Still not sure why you're saying theyve suffered from stagflation over the last few decades
Because they have?  Look up you know... literally anything talking about Japanese economics from before covid, and even most of them between covid and Trump's second term.  You may not like the word, but its the word economists choose to use for the state of Japan's economic for most of the 1990s, 2000s, and 2010s, so that's the one I'm using as well.

You can also look up "Japan's lost decades".  You'll generally get more fluff and less data with that term (given that its meant to evoke emotion rather than economic analysis), but it refers to the same period.

> broke what balance
The balance between raising and lowering interest rates both being "bad" (in the short term where politicians tend to keep their thought patterns).

Trump's "policies" (if you can even call a 3am tweets changing all of US relationships a "policy") have forced up inflation around the world, which forced Japan to finally raise interest rates and break the stagflation cycle.  They'll absolutely suffer for it (same as everyone else who is currently facing inflation in the wake of Trump's actions, including Americans), but it does mean they can't just keep toeing the line like they did for so long.  Even 2008 wasn't enough to break them out of it, despite many economists of the time arguing that it would.

Of course, if Trump's policies are reversed (by himself, by a new congress reimposing limits on his power, or if Japan manages to out-wait him and his successor goes a different route) then Japan may be able to return themselves to stagflation - it just depends if the damage gets "too bad" (loose term I know, deal with it) before they have the opportunity to compensate.

> Not sure why I'd need to be unemployed for half a decade because i support the fiscal expansion?
Because you're only looking at the part of the equation you want to see.  As you're disinclined to trust me, I would again suggest actually looking up the works of real economists from the pre-Trump era.  They'll all tell you the same things I am.

And if you look up more recent research (in the past year or so), you'll see them start talking about the forced changes brought on by unavoidable inflation (of course they'll be written professionally and won't be quite as rude about Trump's antics, but if you read between the lines its always there - not always written in a negative light either, some of them actually still believe Trump has a real plan and not just rage-tariffing whenever he decides he doesn't like someone).

> Lowering rates are not inherently inflationary.
Yes, it is.  Lowering rates means more borrowing and the majority of that borrowed money is created out of thin air.  That's actually a good thing in "normal" times - it gives the country's central bank an extremely potent tool to control the rate of economic growth.

Unfortunately we're not living in "normal" times and inflation is being imposed in a largely uncontrollable manner.  I mean, Trump could control it by ending his tariffs and his failed war in Iran, but his habit is to double down rather than admitting mistakes, so I don't expect either to alleviate any time soon.

In the meantime we're stuck with inflation that's not tied to growth.  Lowering interest rates raises growth, but it also raises inflation even faster.  Raising interest rates slows inflation, but it also slows growth.

That is, if you'll recognize, the _exact formula for stagflation,_ which is why you see so much worry these days about the US (and the rest of the world, for that matter) running into stagflation.

Japan already being in stagflation just gets kicked even harder, which will (or at least has a high chance to) break their cycle but only by putting them in an even worse position in the short term.

Now, I don't think the rest of the world will truly go into stagflation for the simple reason that most of the "uncontrollable" inflationary pressures are trivial to eliminate by just fixing US foreign policy.  There is a time limit on that though (basically when enough importers on both sides have reduced their capacity or just gone out of business that "turning it back on again" becomes a slow process).

> Central banks all around the world after 2008 failing miserably to stimulate inflation with their low rates.
Yeah, by the time you're in full economic meltdown you're well beyond "stimulating inflation".  Businesses that have closed their doors aren't borrowing money no matter how cheap you make it.

> So Japan lowering/keeping rates low doesnt equate to surrendering to inflation by any stretch
It does.  If their problems were as easy to fix as you seem to think, they would have done so 30 years ago.
